listenings.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the program. I'm Professor Hill. I know your reading list is long, so here is my best advice. Don't read every article from the first page to the last. That is the slowest way to read. Start with the abstract. It is the shortest part, and often the most useful. Then skim the conclusion. Ask yourself: is this article important for my question? If it is, read it more carefully. The methods section is usually the most difficult part, so read it last. And please, choose peer-reviewed articles. They are more reliable than blogs or news websites.

Hi, I'm Anna. I'm doing my PhD in marketing in the Netherlands, and I read in English every day. In my first year I used a translator for everything. It was faster, of course. But after six months my English was not better. I didn't learn the words, so every new article was just as difficult. In my second year I changed my method. I read the abstract in English, with no translator. I write down the five most important words, and I only translate a paragraph when it is really necessary. It is slower at the beginning, but now I read much faster than before, and my vocabulary is bigger.

reading.rtitle: How Researchers Read Three Hundred Pages
paras: Many master’s students have the same problem: every week there are hundreds of pages to read, and there is never enough time. The first mistake is to read every article from the first word to the last. It is the slowest method, and it is not the best one. Experienced researchers read in a different order.

First, they read the abstract. It is the shortest part of the article, but it is often the most useful: it gives the question, the sample and the main finding in a few lines. Then they skim the introduction and the conclusion. After that, they decide: is this article important for my work? If the answer is no, they stop. If the answer is yes, they read the rest more carefully, and they scan the tables for the numbers they need.

What about the literature review and the methods? They are usually longer and more difficult than the other parts, so many researchers read them last, and only in the articles that matter. With this method, a student does not read fewer articles. She reads them faster, and she remembers more. And one more tip: a translator is faster, but reading in English builds a better vocabulary for the next article.
